newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PARLIAMENT BACKS TIGHTER UNEMPLOYMENT RULES.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PARLIAMENT BACKS TIGHTER UNEMPLOYMENT RULES.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Friday initially supported bills tightening rules on unemployment benefits to prevent widespread abuses of the social security system.

The draft law, sent to parliamentary committees for further analysis, would remove legal loopholes and make it harder to get an unemployment benefit, Labour Minister Andrzej Baczkowski said earlier this week.
He said many of the 2.5 million officially jobless either collect benefits illegally because they are secretly working, or only qualify because the law is too lax.
Under the new rules a person would first have to work 270 days to qualify for unemployment benefits. Currently, 180 days of work is required.
Unemployed people who engage in temporary, state-subsidised works would not automatically have the right to benefits.
People receiving benefits who are now allowed to take casual jobs paying up to half the minimum wage, would in the future be disqualified if they take any kind of work.
By law, people who lose their jobs are eligible for unemployment benefits of nearly 300 zlotys gross a month for 12 months. The average monthly salary is 920 zlotys.
The government has said that if the new regulations become law the national budget spending for unemployment benefits would be cut by 420 million zlotys next year.
Baczkowski said most of the sum would be spent on creating new jobs and on vocational trainings.
Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said earlier this week that unemployment rate was likely to fall to between 10 and 11 percent at the end of 1997 from the current 13.5 percent.
